title: As ‘American Idol’ Leaves Los Angeles for Atlanta, More Concerns Emerge About the State of Local Production
description:

	In news that felt all too depressingly common in production-starved Los Angeles, wo
body:
Forget Hollywood. “American Idol” is heading to Georgia, dawg.

	In news that felt all too depressingly common in production-starved Los Angeles, word emerged Tuesday that “American Idol” — which has been broadcast live from Los Angeles since it originated in 2002 — would move production to Georgia.

	ABC, as well as producers Fremantle and 19 Entertainment (via owner Sony Pictures TV), didn’t respond to requests for comment about the news. But it makes “American Idol” the latest studio-based reality competition series to pull up stakes and leave Los Angeles in search of tax incentives and lower costs. 
	

	Fox’s “The Masked Singer,” for example, has moved to New Jersey, having most recently shot on the Fox lot in Century City. Also, ABC’s “Shark Tank,” which had been produced on the Sony lot in Culver City, has moved to Atlanta, as has Fox’s “Lego Masters,” formerly shot in Van Nuys. And game shows like “Family Feud” and “Celebrity Family Feud” have also relocated to the Atlanta area.


	The loss of more reality and game series production in California comes even as the state’s film and television tax credit program has expanded to include unscripted fare. But there’s a catch: Those competition shows must have a budget of more than $1 million per episode. That makes it difficult to qualify, even for major shows like “American Idol.”

	The California incentives still don’t include docuseries, talk shows or game shows. States like New Jersey and Georgia, on the other hand, don’t limit their incentives. Georgia’s tax incentives require a total production spend of $500,000, making it more attractive for shows like “American Idol.”
	

	“Reality and unscripted television remain excluded (with the exception of competition shows), despite being one of California’s most productive, scalable, and culturally influential sectors. At a time when producers are navigating shrinking license fees, shorter episode orders, and tighter margins, the ongoing omission of this entire category raises real questions about the long-term viability of keeping these productions in-state,” Weinstein Senior owner Todd Weinstein, Esq., wrote in a post on LinkedIn last year.Reality television has been a foundational part of California’s production economy for decades,” he added. “These shows generate thousands of jobs, support local vendors, keep post facilities running, and increasingly require the same physical infrastructure as scripted content. They might look different with faster schedules, leaner teams, and alternative storytelling structures but they are no less real in terms of economic impact. Still, they continue to sit outside the framework of the tax credit.”

	“American Idol” was broadcast from Television City in the Fairfax district for most of its run; it later shifted to Red Studios Hollywood.

	Deadline was first with the news about “American Idol’s” move to Georgia.

schema.headline: As ‘American Idol’ Leaves Los Angeles for Atlanta, More Concerns Emerge About the State of Local Production

title: Emmys Hit 6.7 Million Viewers, Down 9% From Last Year
description:
NBC’s telecast of the 78th Emmy Awards hit 6.7 million viewers on Monday night, per Nielsen.

	That total marks a 9% decrease from last year’s cerem
body:
NBC’s telecast of the 78th Emmy Awards hit 6.7 million viewers on Monday night, per Nielsen.

	That total marks a 9% decrease from last year’s ceremony on CBS, which brought in 7.4 million viewers — the award show’s best performance since 2021.

	It should be noted, though, that the 2025 ceremony took place on a Sunday, making it easier for viewers to sit down for a three-hour telecast. Compared to the most recent Monday night Emmys — televised by Fox in 2024 — NBC accomplished a 41% increase. But since that telecast, which hit only a meager 4.4 million viewers, was the first in Emmys history to air with fierce competition from an NFL playoff game, the most accurate comparison is perhaps to NBC’s own Monday night Emmys in 2022. In those terms, the network’s latest Emmy efforts made a 10% improvement, up from 5.9 million viewers.
	

	Hosted by “Law & Order: Special Victims Unit” star Mariska Hargitay, the Emmys did air against an NFL game between the Kansas City Chiefs and the Denver Broncos. Even with that competition, it drew enough viewers to rank as the the most-watched non-sports, non-news Monday telecast of 2026, both overall and among adults age 18-49. Hargitay referenced the football game in a pre-recorded sketch featuring a cameo from Taylor Swift, musing that the pop star wouldn’t be able to attend the show because she’d be supporting her husband, Chiefs player Travis Kelce.


	According to NBCUniversal, the Emmys generated 133 million social views, counted across Facebook, Instagram, X and YouTube. The company touts that that marks a 90% increase from 2025.
	

	It appears that this was the Emmys’ last year on a traditional broadcaster. After 31 years of rotating between NBC, CBS, Fox and ABC, the TV Academy is now in talks with Amazon Prime Video.

schema.headline: Emmys Hit 6.7 Million Viewers, Down 9% From Last Year

title: ‘Dancing With the Stars’ Season 35 Kicks Off With Voting Glitch During Premiere
description: “Dancing With the Stars” may have had too many voters than it could handle. After the second dance of the Sept. 15 Season 35 premiere, hosts Juliann
body:
“Dancing With the Stars” may have had too many voters than it could handle. After the second dance of the Sept. 15 Season 35 premiere, hosts Julianne Hough and Alfonso Ribeiro revealed that online voting is down and audiences could only vote via text.

	Then, following the third number, the hosts revealed that all online votes that did go through would be thrown out and only texted votes would count for the first night. And just to complicate things a bit more, there are two different Connor/ers in this competition — so to vote for Conner Leavitt or Connor Wood, viewers need to text Conner L or Connor W.  
	

	This week’s premiere is split into two nights, with Tuesday night for the male celebrities — and one going home at the end of the episode — and Wednesday for the female celebrities and one of them being eliminated. 


	Regardless of the lack of online votes — and only eight couples — there were more than double the number of votes from last year’s premiere.

	At the end of the night, Conner Leavitt was eliminated. Below is a breakdown of all the dances and scores from night one, from top to bottom.

	Harry Shum Jr. and Jenna Johnson — Cha-Cha to “Let’s Groove” by Earth, Wind & Fire21/30

	Ezra Frech and Daniella Karagach — Tango to “Since U Been Gone” by Kelly Clarkson20/30

	Tyler Cameron and Sharna Burgess — Tango to “Are You Gonna Go My Way” by Lenny Kravitz17/30

	Connor Wood and Rylee Arnold — Cha-Cha to “I Like It, I Love It” by Tim McGraw16/30

	Taylor Hanson and Britt Stewart — Quickstep to “Tell Her About It” by Billy Joel16/30
	

	Jackson Olson and Emma Slater — Cha-Cha to “Wannabe” by Spice Girls15/30

	Conner Leavitt and Adele Zaikman — Salsa to “Whoomp! There It Is” by Tag Team12/30

	Guillermo Rodriguez and Witney Carson — Cha-Cha to “Mr. Big Stuff” by Jean Knight10/30

title: Chase Infiniti on TIFF Breakout ‘The Julia Set,’ Love Bombing and Music Video Stardom
description: “The Julia Set” has emerged as one of the biggest surprises of the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival.In her feature debut, writer-director Ni
body:
“The Julia Set” has emerged as one of the biggest surprises of the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival.In her feature debut, writer-director Niki Byrne crafted a perfect showcase for the talents of “One Battle After Another” breakout Chase Infiniti. The latter has earned raves for her turn as a math genius stuck under the thumb of an abusive boyfriend (and an academic system designed to ignore and exploit her).“Julia’s off-the-charts intelligence, which Infiniti embodies with exquisite conviction, changes the stakes of the movie; we’re rooting for her emotional salvation, but we’re also rooting for her to dazzle the universe with her talent,” wrote Variety’s Owen Gleiberman in his TIFF review.Indeed, Infiniti’s wide-eyed portrait of a prodigy is equal parts inspired and frustrating. Julia is recruited by a study group drilling for the Putnam Test — a six-hour math competition for undergraduates considered the most prestigious in the world. When Julia’s teacher’s assistant, Pascal (Christopher Briney), comes on hard and fast with romantic feelings, we watch Infiniti’s Julia struggle to balance blossoming romance with the obligation she has to her extraordinary gifts.Variety caught up with Byrne and Infiniti on the ground in Toronto this week, where the film premiered and is currently shopping for distribution


	Niki, you’ve had an interesting trajectory. You were an aerial photographer and a licensed race car driver. How did we get to writer-director?


	Niki Byrne: Everything I’ve done makes sense in reverse. I came back to California from Europe in 2018 and started working in L.A. I was writing quite a bit at that point, and I knew I wanted to write and direct. I took Martin Scorsese’s master class, where he said that if you’re going to be a director of any quality, you must take acting classes. So, I did and found it super valuable. I’ve worked in almost every department on a film set and found acting incredibly difficult.
	

	Why?

	NB: When acting is done poorly, it’s the easiest job on set. When it’s done well, it’s by far the hardest. I wrote this movie during [COVID] lockdown and came out with this sort of weird confessional script and linked arms with [my producers], and we went on the hunt for our Julia. Then this one walked into a coffee shop in Koreatown.

	Chase, how long ago was that?

	Chase Infiniti: Three years ago. I was a month into shooting “Presumed Innocent.”And you did “One Battle After Another” between then and now, crazy. One of the things that struck me about this performance is how restrained your character is – even in the face of serious abuse and mistreatment from people and systems.
	

	CI: Well, it was a gift getting to bring Niki’s work to the screen. I was instantly drawn to it because Julia is a wonderful human being. It felt like telling a very real story that feels central to growing up. I had a Pascal, of sorts, [in my own life]. Everyone has. I remember a point in time where I was about 18, trying to figure out who I was and scared to show the world my talent. It’s hard to allow yourself to do that.

	I think a lot of people might say that math is the antithesis of artistic work. How much did you have to engage with actual math problems?

	CI: I had to pull from my own experience and flip it in a way that worked for what Julia was going through. I am not a math genius! Math is not my forte. I picked something else in my life that I felt I performed strongly at. I used that to build my confidence with math in the movie.

	And what was that thing you pulled from?CI: I think I’m pretty good at my job. I thought about how I feel about performing in general and used that to create Julia’s energy behind her math skills.

	Another thing that struck me about this film is that it’s one of the clearest examples of “love bombing” I’ve ever seen. There’s a scene where Julia is Pascal a surprise dinner at this apartment, using a key he gave her, and reacts as though she’s robbing the place.

	NB: There were a lot of tears on set that night. Of all the moments we shot, the crew was gently sobbing during that one. We did multiple takes, and he would come in and be so unkind to her, and then she’d break and we’d all be gutted.

	It’s also an important red flag that Pascal is capable of some monstrous things. Chase, not only is your Julia very retreating about her talent – she’s a socioeconomic underdog at her school and a woman of color. How does that inform the character in relation to her wealthy white boyfriend?

	CI: Julia is always doing the next best thing for herself, and also for Pascal. Unfortunately, women of color don’t have the luxury of thinking only about themselves. They’re thinking for everyone around them. This is especially [true] in an abusive relationship. Women of color are some of the most unprotected people in society.

	I have to pivot and ask you about your newfound music video stardom. You were amazing in the Ateez video for “Bad.”

	CI: I just absolutely love them so much. Niki has heard so much about it. The first time we met, I told her she had to listen to them. I made her listen to “Ice on My Teeth.”

	You know everyone’s going to want you to do a musical now that we’ve seen you sing and dance.
	

	CI: I mean – I would love to sing and dance in a musical.

schema.headline: Chase Infiniti on TIFF Breakout ‘The Julia Set,’ Love Bombing and Music Video Stardom

title: ‘Love of Your Life’ Review: Margaret Qualley Goes on a Pretty but Surface-Level Healing Journey
description: It would probably be glib to refer to “Love of Your Life” as “Grieve Pray Love.” Rachel Morrison‘s film about COVID-era loss, recovery and renewal i
body:
It would probably be glib to refer to “Love of Your Life” as “Grieve Pray Love.” Rachel Morrison‘s film about COVID-era loss, recovery and renewal is serious in intent and earnest in execution, grounded by a performance of intelligence and emotional transparency by Margaret Qualley, and doesn’t deserve that kind of easy dismissal. But the temptation is there. It’s hard not to think a little bit of Elizabeth Gilbert’s globe-trotting memoir “Eat Pray Love,” the epitome of breezy Noughties self-help entertainment, not to mention Ryan Murphy’s vapid, glowingly shot film adaptation, when watching this story of a bereaved young woman’s long-term recuperation via perfectly picturesque travels in Lisbon, London, Tokyo and beyond. There’s certainly much to be said for literal escape as a healing strategy, but Morrison’s permanently luminous film too often feels like a magazine spread about that process.
	

	For viewers after a grownup romantic drama with equal, counterbalancing side servings of tearjerking trauma and glossy wish-fulfillment, “Love of Your Life” will handsomely suffice, and ought to rack up considerable streaming numbers when it hits Prime Video on Oct. 14, one month after its Toronto festival premiere. Amazon MGM Studios will also give it a brief theatrical release ahead of that date, but despite the soothing eye-bath of its protagonist’s well-curated world tour, the film never feels altogether cinematic: It’s as attractively mounted as you’d expect from cinematographer-turned-director Morrison (Oscar-nominated for her lensing of “Mudbound”) and her own chosen DP Todd Benhazl (“Hustlers”), but their radiant, exactingly lit images don’t collectively accrue much meaning or power; the film plods through its eight-year timeline with efficient linearity but no particular rhythm.
	

	There’s life inside it, though, and that’s largely thanks to Qualley, a reliably curious and open-hearted actor who can imbue even quite a vaguely drawn character — like the one that screenwriter Julia Cox (“Nyad”) hands her here — with some sense of a soul. When we meet 26-year-old Maya (Qualley), completing a Craigslist purchase of a bedside table from instantly smitten academic Charlie (Gabriel Basso, still in recovery from playing J.D. Vance in “Hillbilly Energy”), she’s barely anybody at all: a nurse, in Boston, with no family she’s willing to mention, and no life outside her grueling hospital shifts. Qualley locates defensive purpose in Maya’s stiff reserve, and an errant gleam of joy when Charlie’s dorky come-ons actually do the job.

	Before long, they’ve moved in together, setting up a perfectly boho-chic love nest in their Victorian apartment. Not too much later, they spring a surprise wedding on their loved ones, to the unspoken but visible consternation of Charlie’s world-weary mom Ruth (ensemble MVP Catherine Keener), and broach the possibility of starting a family — something Maya had always sworn off doing. And all too soon after that, a certain global pandemic strikes, and the worst thing that can happen to our heroine, well, happens. Plunged into the lightless tunnel vision of debilitating grief, she spurns the company of Ruth and longtime best friend Jason (Patrick Schwarzenegger, in a thankless part) and abruptly skips town before anyone can so much as trouble her with funeral arrangements. It’s a selfish trauma response that Qualley, seemingly body-slammed and hollowed-out with pain, makes almost rational.

	Everything that happens from this point on in “Love of Your Life,” however, is considerably harder to swallow. We lurch forward a couple of years to find Maya — now 31 years old, aggressively kohl-eyed and constantly smoking — skulking the gorgeous streets of Lisbon, finding little emotional relief or release in its exquisite painted tiles and pasteis de nata, though plentiful cheap vinho verde is evidently some comfort. But when she meets cute with Felix (Aaron Pierre), an absurdly good-looking touring Brit, she embraces the possibility of romance again, following him first to a Condé Nast-ready holiday home in rural Portugal, and then back to his well-appointed life in West London, complete with adorable young daughter. (He’s a doting single dad on great terms with the girl’s mom, lest you fear this impossible dreamboat may have even a whisper of a character flaw.)
	

	None of this even remotely resembles real life, which makes Maya’s emotional recovery increasingly hard to map: We learn in passing that she’s somehow funding these extended, luxurious travels with a career segue into telehealth, and when her online therapist observes that “we’re really getting somewhere,” we just have to take her word for it. Cox’s script, meanwhile, trades increasingly in one-size-fits-all therapy speak, and despite Qualley’s natural sincerity as a performer, Maya seems steadily less specific a personality as the years pass. 

	Late in proceedings, “Love of Your Life” gets a welcome jolt of feeling and truth from a scene that reunites Maya with Ruth, beautifully played by Keener with all the shattered, visible exhaustion of a woman who hasn’t got to nurture her grief in the Algarve sun. As she unpacks her damage, frankly but no longer angrily, against the unphotogenic greige backdrop of her house’s timber siding, “Love of Your Life” finally reconnects with reality, and not a moment too soon.

schema.headline: ‘Love of Your Life’ Review: Margaret Qualley Goes on a Pretty but Surface-Level Healing Journey

title: Taylor Frankie Paul Sets Return to ‘The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives’ Following Chaotic Season 5 and Ongoing Legal Battle
description:
Taylor Frankie Paul is returning to production on “The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives.”

	Though Hulu declined to comment on Paul’s involvement in Sea
body:
Taylor Frankie Paul is returning to production on “The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives.”

	Though Hulu declined to comment on Paul’s involvement in Season 6, Variety confirmed the news with multiple sources after it was implied in social media posts from cast member Mikayla Matthews, who announced she was quitting the show on Sept. 14.

	Outside of her Season 5 confessionals, Paul hasn’t shot new material for the reality show since March, when production was put on pause due to a police investigation into domestic violence allegations she and her ex-boyfriend Dakota Mortensen made against each other. Shortly thereafter, TMZ released video from a separate domestic incident between them, which led ABC to cancel her season of “The Bachelorette.” Paul and Mortensen have made additional allegations against each other in the months since, leading to mutual restraining orders and a battle for custody over their shared son, Ever. (No charges have been filed in the matter.)
	

	Season 6 recently entered production without Paul. But on Monday, Matthews shared in an Instagram post saying that she was leaving the show after receiving news that upset her, which she implied was related to Paul. On Tuesday, she made another post all but confirming that her exit was a moral objection to Paul’s return.

	Though Matthews didn’t mention Paul by name, she wrote, “The ONLY reason I’m leaving the show is because I was told a certain person was coming back. I told them before agreeing to do 6 that I wasn’t going to film if that certain someone came back. Because it’s UNETHICAL and kids are involved. And I’m being put in an unfair position because of the things I’ve seen and heard that I don’t agree with.”
	

	“Mormon Wives” cast members Mayci Neeley and Layla Taylor may be next to jump ship. Both left comments of support on Matthews’ initial post, and told fans their futures with the show were unclear. “I am finishing this current season that we are filming and then not sure for after that,” Neeley wrote in a TikTok comment after being asked about her status. She then posted a video about material that was cut from the recently released Season 5 with a caption that read, “At the end of the day I don’t care about having ‘aura’ I care about providing for my family and being a good wife/ mother. Period. Going into SLOMW my intention has never been the fame, it has always been $$$ to provide for my fam and to positively impact people by sharing my story. So I’ll take the cut and stay happy & healed.” Responding to a similar fan question about Matthews’ exit, Taylor wrote, “I just love her so much. It’s such an impossible situation for everyone involved, but I am finishing season 6 and then tbd.”

schema.headline: Taylor Frankie Paul Sets Return to ‘The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives’ Following Chaotic Season 5 and Ongoing Legal Battle

title: DOJ Takes Paramount’s Side Against States in Fight Over $1.9 Billion Bond
description: The Department of Justice sided with Paramount on Tuesday, arguing that a coalition of 12 states should be forced to post a bond as the price of con
body:
The Department of Justice sided with Paramount on Tuesday, arguing that a coalition of 12 states should be forced to post a bond as the price of continuing to block the Warner Bros. merger.

	Paramount has argued that it stands to lose at least $1.88 billion due to the delay resulting from the states’ antitrust lawsuit. The company has asked Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin to require the states to post a bond in that amount, which would compensate the company in the event that it prevails at trial.
	

	The DOJ is not a party to the state litigation, but filed a “statement of interest” in the case on Tuesday. The document argues that the states must post a “proper bond” because they are acting in the role of “private persons” in enforcing federal antitrust law.


	The DOJ approved the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger in June and issued an unusual and lengthy statement explaining its support for the transaction. The 12-state coalition, led by California, reached the opposite conclusion in July, filing suit to prevent the merger from reducing competition in the theatrical and basic cable markets. A trial is scheduled to begin on March 2.

	Paramount voluntarily agreed not to close the deal until after a trial is held back in July. At the time, Martinez-Olguin had issued a 28-day temporary restraining order, but had not imposed an injunction that would block the deal indefinitely.

	Rather than fight an injunction motion — and potentially be forced to appeal an adverse ruling — Paramount chose instead to concede the issue and concentrate its trial defense. But the company had a change of heart in August, arguing that the states should be forced to post the bond or, in the alternative, allow the merger to proceed.
	

	In opposing Paramount’s request, the states noted that courts routinely waive the bond requirement when states are suing to enforce public interests. Martinez-Olguin waived the requirement to post a bond when she granted the temporary restraining order.

	The states also argued that requiring states to post a bond would gut their enforcement power. They also argued that Paramount had given no reason why the court should rewrite a stipulation that Paramount had voluntarily acceded to less than a month earlier.

	“Permitting Paramount to enter the stipulation and then rewrite it almost immediately would allow it to unfairly renege on its commitments,” the states argued. “Paramount has failed to show any change in circumstances that would justify its attempt now to rewrite the terms of the stipulation it submitted to the Court.”

	A hearing on the bond request is set for Sept. 24.

	Paramount has separately challenged whether the states have authority to enforce federal antitrust law at all. In a filing last week, the company suggested that one of its defenses will be that such authority “is vested in the U.S. Department of Justice.”

	A court-supervised settlement conference has been set for Oct. 14-15, according to an order issued Tuesday afternoon. A standard part of federal civil litigation, the conference will be confidential. Both sides will have to present their settlement positions to a magistrate judge.

schema.headline: DOJ Takes Paramount’s Side Against States in Fight Over $1.9 Billion Bond

title: How Competitive ‘Pokémon’ Inspired Author Ava Reid’s New Dystopian YA Series ‘Winterveil’
description: It’s the start of another dark academia season and fantasy author Ava Reid (“A Study in Drowning,” “Innamorata”) is celebrating with the release of
body:
It’s the start of another dark academia season and fantasy author Ava Reid (“A Study in Drowning,” “Innamorata”) is celebrating with the release of her new YA dystopian novel, “Winterveil.”

	The first book in a planned duology, “Winterveil” is set at Valeran Academy, which boasts the brightest – and precociously criminal – students in the nation, who are trained to be elite assets in a Cold War that has dragged on for nearly a century. Amid eerie war simulations, cutthroat competitions and foreboding new technology, four students are drawn together for a mysterious mission.
	

	Without getting into spoilers, we can reveal this political tale has one particular inspiration that might come as a surprise: competitive “Pokémon.”


	“I, like so many of us, grew up playing ‘Pokémon’ as a kid,” Reid tells Variety. “Playing ‘FireRed,’ ‘LeafGreen.’ I have all my Pokemon plushies right behind me on my couch right now. But it was during the pandemic that I think so many of us got very involved in kind of esoteric hobbies, and my hobby that I got really into during COVID was competitive ‘Pokémon,’ specifically.”

	And that’s what it sounds like, according to Reid, “’Pokémon’ where you play against you know other players and you have battles.” “And I’m talking specifically about the official competitive format of Pokemon, the one that’s run by the Pokémon Company itself,” Reid says. “There are different fan formats where you can play online, but the official competitive format is called VGC. So I got very, very into VGC, watching a bunch of kind of VGC content creators, playing on the in-game ladder myself.” 
	

	Reid’s time spent playing some hard core Pokemon inspired aspects of the competitive nature of the academy within “Winterveil,” a book that publisher HarperCollins has described as “The Secret History” meets “The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes.”

	“The thing about ‘Pokémon’ is that it works on so many different levels,” Reid says. “There’s a very low skill floor if you just want to engage in the main games and you beat the Elite Four and you catch all the Pokémon. It’s super fun. Pretty much anyone can do it. That’s the aspect of the game that’s marketed toward literal children, but then there’s also competitive Pokemon. It’s a turn-based strategy game, so like chess, but actually many orders of magnitude more complicated than chess. Wolfe Glick, who’s the most famous competitive ‘Pokémon’ player, he’s kind of like the [chess grandmaster] Magnus Carlsen of competitive ‘Pokémon,’ he said that competitive ‘Pokémon’ is like chess, but sometimes the pieces explode, which I think is a great way to explain it. It’s very chesslike. It’s strategic, it’s tactical, but it’s so much more complicated than that. There’s so many ways to customize your ‘Pokémon.’ There’s a lot of math and mathematical equations and probabilities and percentages. So that is the particular element that inspired aspects of ‘Winterveil,’ is competitive ‘Pokémon,’ specifically.”

	When she’s not playing competitive Pokemon, Reid has been hard at work on “Necromantica,” the sequel to her gothic fantasy epic “Innamorata.” After that massive cliffhanger in the first book, which released in March, there’s not much Reid can say yet about the sequel, which debuts next April, except that fan-favorite character Waltrude will certainly return.

	“Waltrude will be back,” Reid says. “She’s a POV character in the sequel, and Marozia is now a POV character in the sequel, which I think is obvious because she’s on the cover. But a large part of the story actually revolves around Gamelyn, who is the Master of Blood, who we’ve not seen very much in the first book. I don’t even think he’s had a line of dialogue, but he is a very, very significant character in the sequel and I’m very excited for that. I think his plot line and his chapters are some of the best things that I’ve ever written. Personally, I believe that, so I’m really excited.”
	

	Elsewhere, Reid is collaborating with “Room” writer Emma Donoghue on a film adaptation of Reid’s 2024 novel, “Lady Macbeth,” told from the point of view of the titular character herself.

	“We’re still pretty early. We’re still working on the script, but things are definitely moving along,” Reid says. “They’re moving along behind the scenes, as so many of these things do, which is kind of a hurry up and wait situation, similar to publishing.”

	Reid isn’t sure what the distribution plans for the film will be, but is not opposed to a streaming launch on the heels of the success of her filmmaker aunt Olivia Newman’s “Remarkably Bright Creatures” on Netflix. The TV movie was nominated for an Emmy at Monday’s awards show and star Sally Field took home the lead actress award in the category.

	“I don’t know if we’re even in the stage to be thinking about that,” Reid says. “I would prefer to have a theatrical release, I think, but my aunt’s movie just came out, ‘Remarkably Bright Creatures,’ and that was on Netflix and that has just done extraordinarily well in that format. So it’s definitely something I’m open to.”

schema.headline: How Competitive ‘Pokémon’ Inspired Author Ava Reid’s New Dystopian YA Series ‘Winterveil’

title: ‘Salvation’ Review: A Pin-Sharp Portrait of an Aspiring Life Coach in Personal Freefall
description: Our first impression of Danny Carlton, the callow protagonist of “Salvation,” is that he doesn’t look like a man you’d trust with your life. He’s yo
body:
Our first impression of Danny Carlton, the callow protagonist of “Salvation,” is that he doesn’t look like a man you’d trust with your life. He’s young, but that’s not the issue. It’s more the palpable air of uncertainty around him, evident in his shallow, darting gaze, his chummy but hesitant speech, his slightly gormless affect; he seems a nice enough lad, eager and solidly gym-built, but you wouldn’t readily hand him any greater responsibility than mowing your lawn. Appearances, of course, can be deceiving, but the great, growing sadness of Tom Nicoll‘s remarkable character study is that, in this case, they’re not. Danny is going nowhere, and just about everyone but him seems to know it, including his mentor and peers on the cockamamie life-coaching course that he thinks will finally make something of him.
	

	A quietly assured and impressive debut for Scottish writer-director Nicoll, “Salvation” is a timely work, in conversation with much recent discourse about the toxic pressures — social, physical and psychological — placed on GenZ men living heavily online. But the film doesn’t feel opportunistically ripped from the headlines. Danny, played with spiraling panic and desperately contrived machismo by a superb Liam Harkins, is a perceptively drawn, tragically human character rather than a representative construct of his time and age. And while his story says much about modern manosphere dynamics, it’s also heavily informed by more constant concerns of British class, gender and geographical difference. 


	There’s much thematic weight here, but balanced throughout with tension and humor — beginning with the all-too-real absurdism of the training retreat where we first meet Danny, and where self-styled life coach Marshall Allison (Kevin O’Loughlin) is fleecing young men for thousands of pounds with the promise that they’ll follow in his footsteps. There’s much jargon-y talk of unlocking freedom and earning potential, repeated with dead-eyed belief by Marshall’s protégés, some with more persuasive swagger than others. Danny is one of the unpersuasive ones, in part because he seems too honest for all this. “It’s not all about the money,” he argues, when Marshall critiques his salesmanship, only to be swiftly corrected by his teacher: “It kind of is.”
	

	Still, at the end of the weekend, Danny gets his certificate, because everyone does — and he returns home to Greenock, a post-industrial coastal town in the Scottish lowlands, an allegedly qualified life coach. Hey, it beats working in a pub, which is what he’s been doing up until now; all he needs is a bit of capital to set up his home office, build his website and secure some advertising, and once the clients come rolling in, he’ll pay back the loans in no time. 

	But apart from Scott (Stephen McMillan), an anxious, socially awkward 22-year-old with even less of a handle on the real world than Danny, no one’s really buying what he’s selling. A handful of other male applicants lose interest fast; he quickly drops his lone female client when she reveals more knowledge of e-commerce than he has. It turns out that even in this dubious professional field, some fakers are faker than others: Danny has mantras and breathing exercises, but no smell of success to him. And when the loan sharks come calling, his barely-a-business plan starts crumbling in wince-inducing fashion.

	In Harkins’ brilliantly twitchy, discomfiting performance, the terror of failure is written across Danny’s smooth, blokey face; so is the woebegone recognition of said failure in just about everything he does. We can hardly miss anything that Danny feels, fears or notices: Nicoll and DP Alex Grigoras shoot much of “Salvation” in tight, peering closeup, made all the more confrontational by the use of cramped Academy ratio throughout. It’s a formal choice that chimes with the character’s routine reliance on his phone’s front-facing camera to put his best face forward, whether in consultation with clients or attempting to hawk his skills on Instagram and TikTok. 

	Life offline could yet save Danny — Kathleen McDermott gives a wonderful, hard-bitten performance as his supportive but unsentimental mom Jackie, who wearily recognizes the limits of her influence — but there’s no promise in Nicoll’s relentlessly screw-tightening script that he’ll ever find his way there. There’s always another internet grift for someone looking to save himself fast, and without any gimmicky visual intrusions, the film feels authentically tuned into the aspirational mentality and oppressive reality of contemporary social media. There’s no need for of-the-moment hectoring or scare-mongering in “Salvation,” however; Danny’s arc on its own feels enough of a cautionary tale.

schema.headline: ‘Salvation’ Review: A Pin-Sharp Portrait of an Aspiring Life Coach in Personal Freefall

title: Viola Davis to Receive San Diego International Film Fest’s Gregory Peck Award for Cinematic Excellence – Film News in Brief
description: Viola Davis will be this year’s recipient of the Gregory Peck Award for Cinematic Excellence at the San Diego International Film Festival. Davis, an
body:
Viola Davis will be this year’s recipient of the Gregory Peck Award for Cinematic Excellence at the San Diego International Film Festival. Davis, an EGOT winner, is being honored for her work as an artist, activist, producer, philanthropist and New York Times bestselling author.

	“Viola Davis is one of the most extraordinary artists of our time,” Tonya Mantooth, CEO and artistic director of San Diego International Film Festival, said. “Her performances bring power, vulnerability and truth to every role, while her work beyond the screen has helped create opportunities for others. The Gregory Peck Award celebrates an enduring contribution to cinema, and Viola Davis embodies that legacy. We are honored to celebrate her remarkable artistry and impact.”
	

	The award, presented by Cecilia Peck, kicks off the 25th year of the festival and will be presented at the Night of the Stars Tribute on Oct. 13. The festival has also announced Jesse Eisenberg’s “The Debut” as the opening night film. The San Diego International Film Festival will take place from Oct. 13-18 in San Diego, California. Passes, tickets and additional festival information are available here.

	
		‘Princess Mononoke’ Returns to Theaters for Studio Ghibli Fest 2026	

	“Princess Mononoke,” from director Hayao Miyazaki, makes its return to theaters.

	The epic fantasy hits the big screen as part of GKIDS and Fathom Entertainment’s Studio Ghibli Fest 2026. A 4K restoration of the film will be in theaters from Sept. 26-30 in both the original Japanese and English-dubbed versions.
	

	The film follows young warrior Ashitaka who encounters a conflict between Lady Eboshi, the people of Iron Town and the mysterious Princess Mononoke. The English dub features the voices of Gillian Anderson, Billy Crudup, Claire Danes, Minnie Driver, Jada Pinkett Smith and Billy Bob Thornton.

	The show dates are below.

	Saturday, Sept. 26 (English language dub)Sunday, Sept. 27 (English language dub)Monday, Sept. 28 (Japanese language with subtitles)Tuesday, Sept. 29 (Japanese language with subtitles)Wednesday, Sept. 30 (English language dub)

title: Tyra Banks: Producers Scoff at Demand For Unedited Miss J Interview Footage
description:
Tyra Banks
                          Fight For Unedited Miss J Interview Footage Turns Ugly
body:
Tyra Banks
                          Fight For Unedited Miss J Interview Footage Turns Ugly
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 15, 2026
                            5:00 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Tyra Banks’ fight for hours of unaired footage shot for the "America’s Next Top Model" documentary is heating up ... with the producers scoffing at the supermodel’s request, TMZ has learned.
      
    
            According to court docs obtained by TMZ, Netflix and the documentary producers are opposing Tyra's attempt to get her hands on the unaired raw footage of her former friends Miss J and Jay Manuel that didn’t end up in the doc.
      
    
            Tyra believes the footage could help prove her claim that she was defamed due to producers selectively editing the interviews.
      
    
            The producers argue Tyra has no right to the raw interview footage, all internal communications about Tyra, all draft scripts, all story notes, and deposition testimony of filmmakers, editors, and others involved in producing or reviewing the documentary. Netflix also had issues with Tyra wanting their internal viewership data. 
      
    
            They insist none of these items are the type of targeted discovery allowed to prove her claims, insisting her requests are way too broad ... particularly at this early stage of the litigation.
